kaigo-atomic-bath-environment.heading: Bathing purposes and checks of environment and condition
paragraphs: Bathing and hygiene remove skin dirt and reduce infection risks, while also supporting freshness, relaxation, satisfaction and daily rhythm. Washing alone does not establish that infection cannot occur; continue necessary precautions. Ask what the person finds comfortable rather than making completion of scheduled bathing the sole purpose.

The textbook describes effects associated with bathing: warming can dilate blood vessels and promote circulation and metabolism, ease muscle or joint pain and movement, and stimulate digestive activity and appetite. Circulation and temperature regulation also change, but effects vary with individual condition. Do not turn these explanations into promises to treat disease or restore joint function. Check whether bathing is suitable and which method fits the person.

Sudden temperature differences between the changing room and bathroom can strain the body. Excessively hot water can also be burdensome, so check room and water temperatures separately. A dry floor does not establish that temperature conditions are safe too.

Inspect slippery floors, steps, routes, supporting points and assistance equipment. Before use, check even familiar equipment for damage or positioning problems. Use the individual plan to confirm an environment and staffing suited to the person’s mobility and sitting abilities.

Before bathing, check that day’s condition and wishes, explain the purpose, actions and necessary assistance, and obtain consent. The material cautions against bathing on an empty stomach or immediately after meals because of effects on digestion and absorption. Check a plan suited to meal times and condition; do not change the caution about immediate post-meal bathing merely to suit staff availability.

Confirm fluids before and after bathing according to condition and plan. Do not recommend the same amount to everyone when drinking has individual conditions. Prepare clothes and towels in advance, and allow the person to choose clothing as far as possible.

An urge to urinate may arise during bathing, so ask beforehand whether the person wants the toilet. This does not mean forcing everyone to eliminate first. Prepare by checking seating, supply placement and which movements the person will perform.

Respect modesty and expose only the areas needed for the current care. Explain necessary observation and privacy screening too. During hygiene care, observe skin within the agreed scope. If redness, pain, wounds or similar changes are found, specifically report their location and condition to healthcare professionals.

If condition changes or assistance cannot proceed safely, do not force continuation to finish the schedule. Request necessary assistance or contact healthcare professionals according to facility procedures. Do not rely solely on written knowledge to perform unfamiliar transfers or bathing assistance.

[Learning comparison] The floor is dry, but the changing room is cold and supporting equipment has not been inspected. Do not assume bathing can start because the floor is dry. Check temperature, equipment, the person’s condition and assistance requirements before explaining the care.

kaigo-atomic-grooming-purpose.heading: Grooming supports individuality and opportunities to choose
paragraphs: Grooming includes washing the face, arranging hair, beard and nail care, changing clothes and oral hygiene. Beyond cleanliness, it can express individuality and support relationships. Do not impose staff preferences for appearance on everyone.

Clothing helps regulate temperature and protect skin. Consider the season, activities and the person’s physical and emotional condition, checking comfort and ease of movement too. Choosing colors or styles from age alone does not capture personal preferences.

Ask about valued habits, makeup and hairstyle preferences, and personal values. Supporting continued dressing and grooming actions the person can perform also uses and helps maintain remaining physical and mental functions. Grooming may support motivation or daily rhythm, but do not promise that changing clothes alone improves every physical and mental function.

Even when dressing assistance is needed, ask about preferred colors and the order of dressing. Preserve independent movements and help only where needed. Receiving physical help does not transfer the right to choose to staff.

Before grooming, specifically confirm what may be done and to what extent. Consent to arrange hair is not consent to all makeup or clothing changes. If the person refuses one part but wants another now, ask about the two separately.

During assistance, avoid unnecessary exposure and check pain, fatigue and wishes to stop. Afterward, check tightness, creases, comfort and skin changes. Fastening every button alone does not establish comfort.

[Learning comparison] The person wants a blue jacket, but the worker recommends another color because of age. First listen to preferences and check safe wearing conditions and today’s activities together. Preserve the opportunity to choose and give only the help required for difficult movements.

kaigo-atomic-home-environment.heading: Connect housework and surroundings with the person’s life
paragraphs: Housework includes cooking, cleaning, laundry, organizing clothes and shopping. It relates to IADL needed to sustain daily life, with widely differing habits and preferences. The number of tasks staff finish alone does not establish that support suits the person’s life.

Cooking connects planning menus, preparing ingredients, cooking, plating, serving and clearing away. When making food easier to eat, check physical condition, illness, allergies and preferences and follow established conditions.

Eating supplies nutrients needed to maintain life and health. Cooking helps adjust ingredients and ease of eating through heat, cutting and other methods. Longer simmering does not mean everyone will absorb nutrients better. Workers must not independently change meal content, texture or treatment-related conditions.

Seasoning and eating habits vary by country and region, and preferences differ even within one region. Seasonal ingredients or ceremonial foods may have personal meaning. New Year’s osechi is one example, not a rule recommending the same food to everyone.

Cleaning removes trash, dust and dirt to create a clean, comfortable living space. Also consider familiar object arrangements and the person’s sense of security. Something staff consider unnecessary may be important to the person.

Before moving or discarding objects, ask which to keep, where to move them and what may be disposed of, and obtain consent. A cleaning request does not allow free movement of personal belongings such as glasses. A person using a wheelchair can still express wishes about their belongings.

Laundry includes sheets and bedding as well as clothing. Check collection, washing according to fabric and labels, drying and return to a clean place as separate stages. Pictures of handwashing or outdoor drying do not prescribe one method for every fabric or establish disinfection through outdoor drying alone.

Items contaminated with blood, stool or vomit must not be handled without protection while waiting for an infection diagnosis. Apply standard precautions and check required protective equipment, hand hygiene and collection methods. Separate dirty and clean flows and match processing to facility procedures and risk.

Unnecessary shaking or spreading of soiled textiles can spread contamination. Handle them as quietly as possible and collect them in designated containers or bags. Do not infer detergent or disinfectant concentration or washing temperature from an illustration; check product, fabric and facility instructions.

Alongside cleanliness, check routes, stairs, bathroom and toilet access, slip resistance and handrails. Watch for raised or curled rug edges that could catch a foot, considering gait and route condition together. A rug’s presence alone does not make every setting safe or unsafe. Temperature, humidity, ventilation, privacy and emotional security also matter. Use suitable assistive equipment to expand activities the person can perform.

[Learning comparison] The room is clean, but the call button is out of reach and staff intend to discard something the person wants to keep. Completed cleaning is insufficient. Check how the person can call when needed and how they want belongings handled, then arrange the environment.

kaigo-atomic-dignity.heading: Understand dignity, independence and quality of life through daily living
paragraphs: Needing care does not remove personal worth or human rights. The person receives support while remaining the agent of their own life. Do not impose staff values as the correct answer for them.

Quality of life (QOL) includes feelings of satisfaction, happiness and purpose. Neither the number of independent actions nor health measurements alone determine whether life is fulfilling. Ask what the person enjoys and values.

Normalization aims for a society in which people with and without disabilities have their rights protected and can live in their own way in the community. It involves removing prejudice and creating opportunities for mutual support, not making everyone’s actions and preferences identical.

Independence has physical and psychological aspects. Even if dressing or mobility requires help, respect thinking about and choosing the desired life. Check remaining abilities and wishes and support the parts that need help.

A day includes getting up, dressing, washing the face, meals, toileting, walking, tea, bathing, sleeping and many other activities. The textbook’s daily schedule is one example. Use it to understand personal rhythms rather than as a rule requiring everyone to act at the same times.

Health, household abilities, housing, family and community or social relationships influence life too. Consider differences in country, culture, customs and experience, and check with the person when supporting them. Do not treat only the life familiar to staff as the standard.

Receiving support can sometimes reduce confidence or motivation. However, do not assume that everyone needing care is passive. Together identify meaningful activities and the parts the person wants to do, supporting initiative while checking safety.

Care workers use professional knowledge and skills to support people whose age, disability or other circumstances make daily living difficult. They observe and cooperate with necessary people to preserve abilities and individual ways of living, rather than deciding everything for the person.

[Learning comparison] The person needs help putting an arm through a sleeve but wants to choose the jacket color. Assisting movement differs from taking over the right to choose. Confirm the preferred color and discuss help with difficult parts.

kaigo-atomic-privacy-abuse.heading: Protect privacy and respond to suspected abuse
paragraphs: Bathing and toileting can expose areas the person does not want others to see. Expose only what is needed for current care and cover the rest. Ask about wishes and explain how necessary observations will be made.

Age, address, medical history, photographs and other personal information do not become freely shareable because you learned them at work. Check the need, recipient and scope of sharing, consent and established procedures. Consent to one task is not consent to photographs or another communication channel.

Do not assume that hiding a name makes posting care developments on personal social media or sending records to private contacts acceptable. Communicate necessary information to designated recipients through established channels, avoiding detailed discussion where others can overhear.

Tying limbs, surrounding a bed with rails to prevent exit, locking someone in, using a belt to prevent standing or excessive medication to suppress behavior can deprive a person of freedom. Examine purpose and actual restriction, not equipment names alone.

Immobilization can reduce physical function and adversely affect mental well-being. Anxiety or confusion may intensify in someone with dementia; restricting movement for safety does not necessarily improve condition. Do not decide the method alone. The organization should consider support without restraints.

Abuse violates human rights. Its five categories are physical abuse, psychological abuse, neglect of care, financial abuse and sexual abuse. Understand them through concrete acts such as hitting and injuring, threats or insults, withholding necessary food or care, improper use of assets and sexual acts without consent.

Several problems can overlap. Withholding food to force obedience, for example, involves both neglected care and frightening interactions that must not be overlooked. Choosing one category does not complete the response; protecting the person takes priority.

If you learn of words or actions suggesting abuse, secure the person’s safety and separately record witnessed or heard facts, times and their own words. Do not wait to protect or consult until you can establish a legal conclusion yourself. With high urgency, immediately seek help or medical care through facility emergency procedures.

Alongside internal reporting routes, confirm appropriate consultation or notification contacts, such as municipal authorities, and procedures for the suspected problem. Do not use privacy as a reason to stop necessary protection or appropriate reporting. Share the necessary scope with the correct office; this material does not replace case-specific legal judgment.

kaigo-atomic-team-roles.heading: Connect professional roles around the person
paragraphs: A multidisciplinary team uses each profession’s expertise around the life the person wants. Physicians handle diagnosis and treatment; nurses provide nursing care and assistance with medical practice. Medical assistance requiring a physician’s or dentist’s instructions must follow those instructions. Care workers observe and communicate daily changes rather than independently diagnosing or changing treatment.

Physical therapists (PT) work with movement functions such as walking; occupational therapists (OT) with activities needed for living; and speech-language therapists (ST) with language, hearing, swallowing and related functions. These roles cooperate; one profession does not replace all others.

Registered dietitians and similar professionals consider nutritional balance, energy requirements and textures and help create suitable menus. Cooking staff prepare meals according to assigned roles and confirmed conditions. Care workers specifically report observed eating, intake amounts and preferences.

Dentists are medical team members who assess and treat teeth and oral conditions. If you hear or observe denture pain or mouth wounds, communicate the location and the person’s complaint for checking. Care workers do not grind dentures to adjust them or independently provide treatment.

Care managers, social workers and related professionals help with daily-life and welfare-service consultation and coordination and plans supporting service use. They talk with the person and contact family or relevant organizations within the necessary scope. Family opinions matter, but do not automatically replace the person’s wishes without asking them.

If eating or swallowing is difficult and today’s texture instructions are unclear, tell the person responsible what was observed and that instructions are unconfirmed. Confirm assessment and the plan with the responsible nurse, registered dietitian, ST and other team members. Workers must not independently change chopping, thickening or energy content.

A coordinated service plan does not prove the service was delivered. Separately share whom you contacted, confirmed conditions and actual results. Distinguishing observations from assumptions supports professional judgment.

[Learning comparison] Knowing the ST role does not increase your authority to independently alter a menu for someone with swallowing concerns. Communicate the person’s condition, clarify who will confirm which instructions and arrange necessary support.

kaigo-atomic-care-process.heading: Care-service forms and evaluation in the care process
paragraphs: In home-visit services, workers visit the person’s home; in day services, the person attends a facility during the day or another designated period. Residential services provide support while the person lives in a facility. Check location, timing and assistance rather than treating names as identical services.

Home help is a home-visit example, day care a day-service example, and a special nursing home for older people a residential example. Knowing these categories does not establish that an individual meets access requirements. Confirm individual eligibility with the person responsible.

The care process starts with gathering information and assessing daily-life issues. Next, plan individual goals and specific support and implement the plan. The process aims to move toward the life the person wants, not merely fill a staff timetable.

After implementation, check the person’s responses and condition and evaluate progress toward goals and whether the plan suited them. The number of interventions or the existence of a written plan alone does not establish effect or goal achievement.

If evaluation identifies missing information, gather it again or review goals and methods. Assessment, planning, implementation and evaluation form a repeating relationship adapted to the person’s life rather than a procedure completed in one direction.

[Learning comparison] A record says a goal was achieved after only scheduling support. Actual assistance, the person’s response and results, and evaluation against the goal are still needed. Check plans, implementation and achievement separately.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-environmen.prompt: Does a dry floor establish that every bathing-safety condition is met?
options: A dry floor removes the need to check water temperature or condition.
Equipment being present removes the need to inspect damage or position.
No. Check temperature differences, water, steps, equipment, personal condition and assistance needs too.
A wish to bathe allows omission of observation or explanation.
rationales: A dry floor is one condition; it does not establish temperature or personal condition.
Equipment presence differs from suitable and safe use for the person.
This checks several aspects of environment and personal condition before arranging support.
Wishes matter but do not authorize omitting necessary explanation or safety conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-grooming-purpos.prompt: The person wants a blue jacket, but the worker thinks only that older people should wear another color. Which support is appropriate?
options: Staff choose by age and tell the person after dressing.
Ask preferences, check season, activity and condition, and assist necessary movements.
Needing dressing help transfers color choices to staff too.
Because the person chose the color, omit comfort and pain checks.
rationales: Age-based assumptions fail to respect individuality and choice.
This starts with wishes and checks actual wearing conditions and necessary help.
Assisting movement differs from transferring decision-making rights to staff.
Respecting choice does not remove checks of condition and comfort after dressing.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-home-environmen.prompt: The room is clean, but the call button is out of reach and the person does not want belongings discarded. Which response is appropriate?
options: Record the living environment as complete because cleaning is done.
Discard anything staff consider unnecessary without asking.
Explain the button’s name and omit reach checks.
Check a usable way to call and wishes for belongings, arranging safety, security and the scope of consent.
rationales: Cleanliness leaves contact access and security unresolved.
Items may be important; confirm wishes and consent before disposal.
Explaining function does not prove the person can reach and use it.
This considers usability and choice alongside cleanliness.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dignity.prompt: The person needs help putting on a jacket but wants to choose its color. Which support for independence is appropriate?
options: Staff choose all colors because assistance is needed.
Choosing a color means necessary dressing assistance should be withheld.
Preserve choice and independent movements and help with difficult parts.
Use another person’s preferred color without asking.
rationales: Physical help does not remove the right to choose.
Deciding independently differs from performing every movement independently.
This respects psychological independence and retained abilities while providing necessary help.
Check with the person rather than substituting others’ preferences.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-privacy-abuse.prompt: You learn that necessary food is withheld to force obedience. Which understanding and response are appropriate?
options: Suspect neglect and psychological harm, protect safety and report witnessed or heard facts to an appropriate contact.
Food may be used for discipline, so necessary support can stop.
Do not protect or consult until you establish the legal conclusion yourself.
It is a staff issue, so omit the person’s condition and words from records.
rationales: This recognizes withheld essential food and frightening treatment and arranges safety and appropriate consultation or reporting.
Using food as punishment or control while omitting necessary care is inappropriate support.
Safety and consultation are needed even at suspicion; do not wait for your own legal determination.
Check effects on the person and record facts separately from their words.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-team-roles.prompt: Swallowing is a concern and today’s food texture is unconfirmed. What should a care worker who knows the ST role do?
options: Knowing the ST role authorizes independent fine chopping.
Judge texture from appearance and omit the individual plan.
Use one texture for everyone without reporting the person’s condition.
Report observations and unconfirmed instructions to the person responsible and confirm professional assessment and the current plan.
rationales: Knowing a role does not authorize independent changes to meal conditions.
Appearance alone cannot establish suitability for abilities or instructions.
Uniform treatment without individual checks is inappropriate.
This shares observations and confirms support with nurses, registered dietitians, STs and other professionals.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-care-process.prompt: Support has only been scheduled, but “goal achieved” was recorded. What still needs checking?
options: Only the fact that information was collected and a plan written.
Actual assistance, the person’s responses and results, and evaluation against the goal.
Only the scheduled intervention count, without checking personal changes.
Writing goals and assistance means evaluation is complete too.
rationales: Collecting information and writing belong to assessment and planning. Achievement requires checking actual assistance and results.
Plans, implementation, results and evaluation are separate. Confirm assistance and responses, then compare actual change with the goal.
Intervention counts describe the process, but alone do not establish personal results or progress.
Writing goals and specific support is planning. Evaluation checks fit and achievement against results after implementation.
